'''Robert Howard Crabtree''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}}<ref name=frs/> (born 17 April 1948) is a British and American [[chemist]]. He is serving as Conkey P. Whitehead Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at [[Yale University]] in the United States. He is a naturalized citizen of the United States.<ref>[http://ursula.chem.yale.edu/~crabtree/CV_May_08.pdf Yale Faculty webpage]{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. Retrieved 21 September 2014</ref> Crabtree is particularly known for his work on "[[Crabtree's catalyst]]" for hydrogenations, and his textbook on [[organometallic chemistry]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20051222143000/http://ursula.chem.yale.edu/~crabtree/ Crabtree Lab Homepage], ursula.chem.yale.edu. Retrieved 21 September 2014.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |editor-first1=Robert H. |editor-last1=Crabtree |title=The Organometallic Chemistry of the Transition Metals |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781118788301 |date=2014 |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781118788301|isbn=978-1-118-13807-6 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Education==
Robert Howard Crabtree studied at [[Brighton College]] (1959–1966), and earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from the [[University of Oxford]], where he was a student at [[New College, Oxford]] in 1970, studying under [[Malcolm Green (chemist)|Malcolm Green]]. He received his PhD from the [[University of Sussex]] in 1973, supervised by [[Joseph Chatt]].<ref name=PhD-452454>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Sussex|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/42715203?style=html|title=Transition Metal Dinitrogen Complexes Adduct Formation and Base Character|first=Robert Howard|last=Crabtree|year=1973|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.452454}}|archive-date=16 June 2018|access-date=16 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180616130624/https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/42715203?style=html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
After his PhD, Crabtree was a [[postdoctoral researcher]] with [[Hugh Felkin]] at the [[Institut de Chimie des Substances Naturelles]] at [[Gif-sur-Yvette]], near Paris. He was a postdoctoral fellow (1973–1975) and then attaché de recherche (1975–1977). At the end of that time he was chargé de recherche. In 1977 Crabtree took an assistant professorship in Inorganic Chemistry at [[Yale University]]. He served as associate professor from 1982 to 1985, and as full professor from 1985 to 2021.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dobereiner|first1=Graham E.|last2=Hazari|first2=Nilay|last3=Schley|first3=Nathan D.|date=2021-02-08|title=Pioneers and Influencers in Organometallic Chemistry: Professor Robert Crabtree's Storied Career via an Unusual Journey to the Ivy League|journal=Organometallics|volume=40|issue=3|pages=295–301|doi=10.1021/acs.organomet.0c00797|s2cid=234003600|issn=0276-7333|doi-access=free}}</ref> In retirement, he now serves as an emeritus professor of chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Robert Crabtree {{!}} Department of Chemistry|url=https://chem.yale.edu/faculty/robert-crabtree|access-date=2021-11-21|website=chem.yale.edu|language=en}}</ref>

==Research==
===Hydrogenation===
Crabtree is renowned for his influential work on [[hydrogenation]], particularly his contributions to the development of the [[Crabtree catalyst]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crabtree |first1=Robert H. |last2=Felkin |first2=Hugh |last3=Morris |first3=George E. |title=Activation of molecular hydrogen by cationic iridium diene complexes |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications |date=1 January 1976 |issue=18 |pages=716–717 |doi=10.1039/C39760000716 |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1976/c3/c39760000716 |language=en |issn=0022-4936|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This catalyst, utilizing [[iridium]] as the active metal, displays exceptional efficiency, regio- and stereoselectivity in hydrogenation reactions. Notably, when terpinen-4-ol undergoes hydrogenation, the Crabtree catalyst exhibits a remarkable preference of 1000:1 for adding [[hydrogen]] to the substrate face containing the OH group. In contrast, the hydrogenation reaction with [[Palladium on carbon]] only achieves a selectivity ratio of 20:80. The [[chelation]] of the [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]] to the [[catalyst]] is evident from the identification of a catalyst-substrate complex involving norbornene-2-ol.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crabtree |first1=Robert H. |last2=Davis |first2=Mark W. |title=Occurrence and origin of a pronounced directing effect of a hydroxyl group in hydrogenation with [Ir(cod)P(C6H11)3(py)]PF6 |journal=Organometallics |date=May 1983 |volume=2 |issue=5 |pages=681–682 |doi=10.1021/om00077a019 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/om00077a019 |language=en |issn=0276-7333|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crabtree |first1=Robert H. |last2=Davis |first2=Mark W. |title=Directing effects in homogeneous hydrogenation with [Ir(cod)(PCy3)(py)]PF6 |journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry |date=July 1986 |volume=51 |issue=14 |pages=2655–2661 |doi=10.1021/jo00364a007 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jo00364a007 |language=en |issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[File:Selective Hydrogenation.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Selective Hydrogenation of terpinen-4-ol utilizing Crabtree's Catalyst.]]

[[File:Iridium dehydrogenation.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Stoichiometric alkane dehydrogenation of cyclooctane with tert-butylethylene as a hydrogen acceptor.]]

During his early research, Crabtree also focused on [[C–H bond activation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Burk |first1=Mark J. |last2=Crabtree |first2=Robert H. |title=Selective catalytic dehydrogenation of alkanes to alkenes |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=December 1987 |volume=109 |issue=26 |pages=8025–8032 |doi=10.1021/ja00260a013 |bibcode=1987JAChS.109.8025B |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja00260a013 |language=en |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Crabtree's groundbreaking contribution in this area was reversing the [[hydrogenation]] reactions he developed before, particularly in stoichiometric [[alkane]] [[dehydrogenation]]. He utilized tert-butylethylene as a hydrogen acceptor to facilitate the release of hydrogen during the dehydrogenation of [[cyclooctane]], forming bound [[cyclooctadiene]]. This discovery demonstrated one of the earliest instances of [[intermolecular]] [[C–H activation]] using a [[homogeneous]] [[metal complex]]. This achievement played a significant role in his [[tenure]] award and academic success

===A novel form of Hydrogen Bonding===

[[File:Unconventional hydrogen bonding in transition metal hydrides complexes.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Unconventional hydrogen bonding in transition metal hydrides complexes.]]

Another part of Crabtree's research centers on a novel form of [[hydrogen bonding]] that involves [[metal hydrides]], resulting in unconventional bonding interactions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crabtree |first1=Robert H. |title=A New Type of Hydrogen Bond |journal=Science |date=11 December 1998 |volume=282 |issue=5396 |pages=2000–2001 |doi=10.1126/science.282.5396.2000 |s2cid=93959077 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.282.5396.2000 |language=en |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klooster |first1=Wim T. |last2=Koetzle |first2=Thomas F. |last3=Siegbahn |first3=Per E. M. |last4=Richardson |first4=Thomas B. |last5=Crabtree |first5=Robert H. |title=Study of the N−H···H−B Dihydrogen Bond Including the Crystal Structure of BH 3 NH 3 by Neutron Diffraction |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1 July 1999 |volume=121 |issue=27 |pages=6337–6343 |doi=10.1021/ja9825332 |bibcode=1999JAChS.121.6337K |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja9825332 |language=en |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Traditional hydrogen bonds feature a [[protic]] hydrogen donor and an [[electronegative]] acceptor, while Crabtree's discoveries include [[aromatic ring]] [[π electrons]] as weaker acceptors in X–H···π hydrogen bonds (X = N, O). Surprisingly, Crabtree also observed Y–H σ bonds (Y= B or metal) acting as acceptors, leading to X–H···H–Y structures with significantly shorter H···H distances compared to typical contacts. Known as "dihydrogen bonds," these interactions exhibit bond lengths of approximately 1.8 Å, in contrast to the regular H···H length of 2.4 Å. Crabtree's findings shed light on the diverse nature of hydrogen bonding, with implications for understanding molecular structures and designing [[catalysts]] with tailored properties.

===Introduction of Mesoionic Carbenes===

[[File:C4 coordinated imidazolylidene Iridium complex in transfer hydrogenation catalysis.png|thumb|upright=1.3|C4 coordinated imidazolylidene Iridium complex in transfer hydrogenation catalysis.]]

Crabtree has made significant contributions to the field of [[carbene]] chemistry, particularly in the exploration of mesoionic carbenes (MICs), or so called "abnormal carbenes". These carbenes, offer advantages as ligand systems in organometallic complexes and catalytic applications. Unlike C2 coordinated imidazolylidenes, mesoionic carbenes possess only charge-separated electronic [[resonance structures]], allowing for greater adaptability to metal centers within [[catalytic]] cycles. Crabtree has developed novel methods for generating and isolating abnormal carbenes, providing insights into their structures and stability under different conditions. Notably, he introduced the first example of an abnormal carbene complex incorporating an [[iridium]] complex with a C4 coordinated imidazolylidene, which found application in transfer hydrogenation catalysis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gründemann |first1=Stephan |last2=Kovacevic |first2=Anes |last3=Albrecht |first3=Martin |last4=Robert |first4=Jack W. Faller |last5=Crabtree |first5=H. |title=Abnormal binding in a carbene complex formed from an imidazolium salt and a metal hydride complex |journal=Chemical Communications |date=23 October 2001 |issue=21 |pages=2274–2275 |doi=10.1039/B107881J |pmid=12240147 |url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2001/cc/b107881j |language=en |issn=1364-548X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Manganese di-μ-oxo Dimers for Oxygen Evolution===

[[File:Manganese di-μ-oxo dimers involved in O2-evolution as a functional model for photosynthetic water oxidation.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Manganese di-μ-oxo dimers involved in O2-evolution as a functional model for photosynthetic water oxidation.]]

Crabtree's research has made significant advancements in our understanding of O–O bond formation within [[manganese]] di-μ-oxo dimers involved in [[oxygen evolution]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Limburg |first1=Julian |last2=Vrettos |first2=John S. |last3=Liable-Sands |first3=Louise M. |last4=Rheingold |first4=Arnold L. |last5=Crabtree |first5=Robert H. |last6=Brudvig |first6=Gary W. |title=A Functional Model for O-O Bond Formation by the O 2 -Evolving Complex in Photosystem II |journal=Science |date=5 March 1999 |volume=283 |issue=5407 |pages=1524–1527 |doi=10.1126/science.283.5407.1524 |pmid=10066173 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.283.5407.1524 |language=en |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Limburg |first1=Julian |last2=Vrettos |first2=John S. |last3=Chen |first3=Hongyu |last4=de Paula |first4=Julio C. |last5=Crabtree |first5=Robert H. |last6=Brudvig |first6=Gary W. |title=Characterization of the O 2 -Evolving Reaction Catalyzed by [(terpy)(H 2 O)Mn III (O) 2 Mn IV (OH 2 )(terpy)](NO 3 ) 3 (terpy = 2,2':6,2' '-Terpyridine) |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=1 January 2001 |volume=123 |issue=3 |pages=423–430 |doi=10.1021/ja001090a |pmid=11456544 |bibcode=2001JAChS.123..423L |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja001090a |language=en |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Through his investigations, he has put forward a simplified proposal for the [[reaction mechanism]] responsible for the generation of [[oxygen]] through the reaction of a manganese di-μ-oxo dimer with [[NaClO]]. The oxidation of the IV/IV dimer results in the production of a Mn(V)=O dimer. Subsequently, the formation of the O–O bond could potentially occur through a [[nucleophilic attack]] of OH– on the oxo group. Oxygen-18 [[isotope]] labeling experiments have demonstrated that the oxygen atoms in the evolved molecular oxygen originate from [[water]]. This system thus serves as a functional model for photosynthetic water oxidation.

Crabtree has made significant contributions in [[C–H bond activation]], water oxidation, and [[hydrogenation]]. His approach entails selecting unique projects, conducting early critical experiments, transitioning between problems, developing air-stable catalysts, and educating through his writing.
